Biology:

Genetics

and

Cell

Division

DNA

is

the

molecule

that

contains

the

genetic

instructions

used

by

living

organisms.

Genes

are

sections

of

DNA

that

provide

instructions

for

making

proteins

and

other

molecules

needed

by

cells.

DNA

is

organized

into

structures

called

chromosomes.

Humans

normally

have

46

chromosomes,

arranged

into

23

pairs.

Traits

can

be

influenced

by

the

genes

an

individual

inherits

from

their

biological

parents.

Cells

reproduce

through

a

process

called

cell

division.

Mitosis

produces

two

genetically

identical

daughter

cells

and

is

important

for

growth,

development,

and

repairing

damaged

tissues.

Before

mitosis

occurs,

the

cell

copies

its

DNA

so

that

each

new

cell

receives

a

complete

set

of

genetic

information.

Meiosis
,

on

the

other

hand,

produces

reproductive

cells

such

as

eggs

and

sperm.

Meiosis

results

in

cells

with

half

the

normal

number

of

chromosomes

and

creates

genetic

variation

among

offspring.

Biology:

Ecosystems

and

Energy

An

ecosystem

includes

living

organisms

and

the

nonliving

parts

of

their

environment.

Organisms

interact

with

each

other

through

relationships

such

as

competition,

predation,

and

cooperation.

Producers,

such

as

plants,

create

their

own

food

through

photosynthesis.

Consumers

obtain

energy

by

eating

other

organisms,

while

decomposers

break

down

dead

organisms

and

return

nutrients

to

the

environment.

Energy

moves

through

an

ecosystem

in

a

food

chain

or

food

web.

For

example,

grass

may

be

eaten

by

a

rabbit,

which

may

then

be

eaten

by

a

fox.

At

each

level

of

the

food

chain,

some

energy

is

used

by

organisms

for

movement,

growth,

and

other

activities,

while

some

is

lost

as

heat.

Because

less

energy

is

available

at

higher

levels

of

a

food

chain,

ecosystems

generally

contain

more

producers

than

top-level

predators.

Cells are the basic units of life. All living organisms are made of one or more cells. There are two main types of cells: prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, do not have a nucleus. Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus that contains the cell's genetic material. Eukaryotic cells are found in organisms such as plants, animals, fungi, and protists.
Cells contain different organelles that perform specific jobs. The nucleus stores DNA and controls many of the cell's activities. Mitochondria produce energy for the cell through cellular respiration. Ribosomes make proteins, while the cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell. Plant cells also contain chloroplasts, which allow plants to perform photosynthesis. During photosynthesis, plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to produce glucose and oxygen.
